title: The Last Train to the Coast
summary: A family nearly misses their holiday train, but the children help solve the problem by reading the schedule and asking the station staff.
poll: Children can help solve a family problem just as well as adults can.

versions.title: The Last Train to the Coast
versions.text:
Sara and Omar want to see their grandparents. They live by the coast. The family must catch a train. It is a holiday trip.

Every year, they check the train times. They learn to read the big board. They learn about the train tracks. The board shows every train.

Today, they leave very late. Dad drives fast to the station. But the road is slow. There are many cars.

They run inside the station. They look at the board. Sara reads it fast. Their train is gone!

They must find a new way. They need another train. The last train leaves soon. They do not have much time.

A worker walks by. Omar asks him fast. "Is there one more train?" The worker checks his list.

"Yes! One more train," he says. "It leaves from a new track." The family runs to find it.

They reach the train just in time! They sit down and smile. "We did it together," says Sara. The train goes to the coast.

versions.title: The Last Train to the Coast
versions.text:
Sara and her younger brother Omar want to see their grandparents, who live in a small town by the coast. The family must catch a train today. It is a special holiday trip that the family has planned for weeks.

Every year, the family sits down and checks the train times together. The kids have learned to read the busy board on their own. They have also learned about the different train tracks at the station. The board shows every single train and its time.

Today, though, they leave the house much later than planned. Dad drives as fast as he safely can toward the station. But the road leading into town is slow this morning. There are far too many cars on the road ahead.

They hurry inside the busy station and look up right away. They search the large board closely for their train. Sara reads through the list of train times quickly. "Our train has already left!" she says, clearly worried.

Now the family must find another way to reach the coast. They need to catch a different train instead. The last train of the night leaves fairly soon. They do not have much time left to decide.

Just then, a station worker happens to walk by them. Omar quickly stops him and asks a question. "Excuse me, is there one more train tonight?" The worker checks his list very carefully.

"Yes, there is still one more train tonight," he says kindly, smiling at the children. "It leaves soon from a different track." The whole family runs quickly to find it.

They reach the correct train just in time, breathless! They sit down together, relieved and smiling warmly. "We solved this tricky problem together," says Sara proudly. The train speeds steadily onward toward the sunny coast.

versions.title: The Last Train to the Coast
versions.text:
Sara and her brother Omar live with their parents in a busy city. Their grandparents live far away, by the coast. Today is a special holiday. The whole family must catch an important train to visit them.

Each year before this trip, the family studies the train times together. The children have learned how to read the busy board on their own. They have also learned about the many different tracks. Each track leads to a different part of the country.

Today, though, everything seems to go wrong at once. Dad cannot find his phone anywhere in the house. Worried about being late, Mom hurries everyone out the door and into the car.

On the road into town, traffic crawls along slowly. Dad grips the wheel tightly, glancing at the clock again and again. By the time they reach the station, only a few minutes remain before their train was due to leave.

Sara understands right away that something has gone wrong. Rushing inside, she scans the long list of times and gasps. Their train has already left without them!

Taking a deep breath, Omar remembers what his parents taught him about train stations. He quickly spots a worker nearby. "Excuse me, is there another train leaving tonight?" he asks politely, trying to stay calm.

The worker checks his list and smiles. "You are lucky. One more train leaves soon, from a different platform." The whole family dashes toward the new platform as fast as they can.

They reach the platform just as the doors are closing, and they climb aboard together, breathless. By the time the train pulls away, Sara and Omar are smiling at each other with quiet pride.

versions.title: The Last Train to the Coast
versions.text:
In a busy city far from the quiet coastal town where their grandparents live, Sara and her brother Omar wake early for a special holiday trip. Today, the whole family must catch an important train, since missing it would mean losing an entire day of their visit.

Each year before this same trip, the family sits down together and studies the train schedule carefully. The children have learned to read the crowded arrivals board entirely on their own. They have also learned about the many different platforms, since each one serves a different region of the country.

Today, however, everything seems to unravel at almost the same moment. Dad cannot locate his phone anywhere in the house, despite searching every obvious place. Worried about the growing delay, Mom hurries everyone out the door and into the waiting car.

On the road leading into the city center, traffic crawls forward in frustrating little bursts. Dad grips the steering wheel tightly, glancing repeatedly at the dashboard clock. By the time they finally reach the crowded station, only a few precious minutes remain before their scheduled train was due to depart.

Sara senses immediately that something has gone wrong, even before she reaches the arrivals board. Rushing inside, breathless, she scans the long list of departure times and gasps aloud. Their train has already left without them.

Drawing a steadying breath, Omar remembers what their parents have patiently taught them about navigating busy stations. He quickly spots a station worker nearby, carrying a clipboard. "Excuse me, is there another train leaving tonight?" he asks, forcing himself to stay calm despite the mounting panic.

The worker checks his schedule carefully and smiles reassuringly at the anxious children. "You are fortunate," he says. "One more train departs soon, from a different platform across the station." The whole family dashes toward the distant platform as quickly as they possibly can.

They reach the platform just as the doors begin sliding shut, climbing aboard together, utterly breathless. As the train finally pulls away into the gathering evening, Sara and Omar exchange a quiet, satisfied smile.

versions.title: The Last Train to the Coast
versions.text:
In a busy city far from the quiet coastal town where their grandparents live, Sara and her brother Omar wake early for a special holiday trip, knowing they must not be late. Today, the whole family must catch an important train, since missing it would mean losing an entire day of their carefully planned visit.

Each year before this same trip, the family sits down together and studies the train schedule with great care, treating it almost like a shared ritual. The children have learned to read the crowded arrivals board entirely on their own initiative, without needing any help from their parents. They have also learned about the many different platforms, since each one serves a distinct region of the country and leads to an entirely different destination.

Today, however, everything seems to unravel at almost the same unfortunate moment. Dad cannot locate his phone anywhere in the house, despite searching every obvious hiding place with growing frustration. Worried about the rapidly growing delay, Mom hurries everyone out the door and into the waiting car outside, calling instructions over her shoulder.

On the road leading into the city center, traffic crawls forward in frustrating little bursts, never quite gaining any real speed. Dad grips the steering wheel tightly, glancing repeatedly at the dashboard clock as the minutes tick away. By the time they finally reach the crowded station, only a few precious minutes remain before their scheduled train was due to depart entirely.

Sara senses immediately that something has gone wrong, even before she reaches the distant arrivals board across the hall. Rushing inside, utterly breathless, she scans the long list of departure times and gasps aloud in genuine dismay. Their train has already left without them, pulling away minutes earlier.

Drawing a steadying breath to calm his racing thoughts, Omar remembers what their parents have patiently taught them about navigating busy, unfamiliar stations. He quickly spots a station worker standing nearby, carrying a clipboard tucked under one arm. "Excuse me, is there another train leaving the station tonight?" he asks, forcing himself to stay calm despite the mounting panic rising inside him.

The worker checks his schedule carefully and smiles reassuringly down at the anxious children standing before him. "You are rather fortunate," he says kindly, glancing at his watch. "One more train departs soon, from a different platform clear across the station." The whole family dashes toward the distant platform as quickly as they possibly can manage.

They reach the platform just as the doors begin sliding slowly shut, climbing aboard together in one last desperate rush, utterly breathless from running. As the train finally pulls away into the gathering evening sky, Sara and Omar exchange a quiet, satisfied smile of genuine relief.

keyWords.definition: a building where trains stop so people can get on or off
keyWords.example: We waited for the bus at the station.

keyWords.definition: a big sign that shows information, like train times
keyWords.example: She checked the board to find her flight.

keyWords.definition: the metal path that a train runs along
keyWords.example: The train rolled slowly down the track.

keyWords.definition: a special day or trip away from school or work
keyWords.example: We went to the beach for our summer holiday.

keyWords.definition: a person who has a job, especially one that helps others
keyWords.example: A worker at the store helped us find the milk.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A family who almost misses their train but finds another one
A family who decides never to take the train again after the trip
A family who wins a prize at the train station for being on time
A family who moves to a new house by the coast near the sea
questions.why: The story follows the family almost missing their train and then catching a later one.

wrong.B: The family still wants to take the train at the end.
wrong.C: The story does not mention winning a prize.
wrong.D: The family is visiting, not moving.

questions.stem: Why does the family leave the house late?
options: Because they forgot to pack any bags
Because the train station was closed for the day
Because Dad could not find his phone anywhere
Because they wanted to eat breakfast first
questions.why: The story says Dad searches the house for his missing phone, which makes them late.

wrong.A: Mom packs the bags; they are not forgotten.
wrong.B: The station is open; their train just leaves without them.
wrong.D: The story does not mention breakfast.

questions.stem: What happens right after the family reaches the station?
options: They buy tickets for a different holiday trip
They call their grandparents on the phone to say hello
They ask a worker to drive them home in a van today
They look at the board and see their train is gone
questions.why: The story says they rush inside and read the board, where they see their train has already left.

wrong.A: They are not buying tickets for a new holiday.
wrong.B: The story does not show them calling their grandparents.
wrong.C: No one asks the worker to drive them anywhere.

questions.stem: In the story, a track is —
options: a kind of holiday gift
the path a train runs on
a worker at the station
a loud train horn
questions.why: The story talks about different tracks, meaning the paths trains run along.

wrong.A: A track is not a gift.
wrong.C: A track is not a person.
wrong.D: A track is not a sound.

questions.stem: Why must the family find another train?
options: Because they want to visit a different city
Because the first train broke down completely
Because they missed their first train
Because the weather was too stormy to travel
questions.why: Since their first train already left, the family must find another way to reach the coast.

wrong.A: They still want to go to the same coastal town.
wrong.B: The story does not say the train broke down.
wrong.D: The story does not mention a storm.

questions.stem: How does Sara feel when she sees the board?
options: Worried, because their train has already left
Happy, because the train is early today
Bored, because the station is empty and quiet
Angry, because her brother is slow to pack
questions.why: The story shows Sara gasping when she sees their train is already gone, showing worry.

wrong.B: Their train is gone, not early.
wrong.C: The station is busy and crowded, not empty.
wrong.D: Sara is not angry at Omar.

questions.stem: Why does Omar ask the worker a question?
options: He wants to buy a snack at the station
He wants to know the time in another city
He wants directions to the bathroom
He wants to know if there is another train
questions.why: Omar asks the worker whether another train is leaving that night, so the family can still go.

wrong.A: Omar is not asking about snacks.
wrong.B: Omar is not asking about another city's time.
wrong.C: Omar is not asking for directions.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story with Sara and Omar smiling?
options: To show that the train ride was boring
To show that the children helped solve the problem
To show that they missed the trip completely
To show that their parents were angry at them for leaving
questions.why: The smile shows the children feel proud that their question helped the family catch the train.

wrong.A: The story does not say the ride is boring.
wrong.C: The family does not miss the trip; they board the train.
wrong.D: The story does not show the parents being angry.

LOW.prompt: Would you have thought to ask a worker for help like Omar did? Explain your answer using at least two details from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two details from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think I would ask a worker for help like Omar did. He stayed calm even though their train was already gone. He also remembered that workers at the station can help with questions. If I were in that situation, I think asking for help would be the smart thing to do, just like Omar did.

keyWords.definition: the raised area at a station where people wait to get on a train
keyWords.example: We waited on the platform until our train arrived.

keyWords.definition: the cars and other vehicles moving along a road
keyWords.example: Heavy traffic made us ten minutes late for school.

keyWords.definition: a device used to call or message other people
keyWords.example: She used her phone to text her mom.

keyWords.definition: out of breath, usually from running or hurrying
keyWords.example: He arrived breathless after sprinting up the stairs.

keyWords.definition: to move or act very quickly
keyWords.example: We had to rush to catch the last bus home.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: The family decides train travel is too stressful to continue, so they go home by car in the night
The grandparents decide to come to the city instead, so the children no longer need any train
The train breaks down before it ever leaves, and the children go back home that night
The children use the schedule and ask for help to catch the last train
questions.why: The story centers on the children's knowledge and quick thinking helping the family catch the final train.

wrong.A: The family still plans this trip every year.
wrong.B: The grandparents stay at the coast the whole story.
wrong.C: The train is never described as broken.

questions.stem: What do the children already know how to do, from past trips?
options: Read the board and understand the platforms
Drive the family car all the way to the station
Fix a broken phone quickly during the trip
Talk to each worker at the station by name
questions.why: The story says the children have learned to read the board and understand the platforms on their own.

wrong.B: The children do not drive the car.
wrong.C: No one fixes the phone; it is simply missing.
wrong.D: The story does not say they know every worker by name.

questions.stem: What causes the family to be late leaving the house?
options: Heavy rain flooding the street outside
A flat tire on the family car
Dad cannot find his phone anywhere
Mom forgets where the station is
questions.why: The story explains that searching for Dad's missing phone delays the whole family.

wrong.A: The story does not mention rain or flooding.
wrong.B: The story does not mention a flat tire.
wrong.D: Mom knows exactly where the station is.

questions.stem: In the story, breathless means —
options: feeling calm and relaxed
out of breath from running hard
unable to speak any language
wearing a warm winter coat
questions.why: The family is breathless after rushing and running to reach the new platform in time.

wrong.A: Breathless is the opposite of calm and relaxed.
wrong.C: Breathless does not mean unable to speak a language.
wrong.D: Breathless has nothing to do with clothing.

questions.stem: Why does traffic make the family more worried?
options: It eats into the little time they have left before the train leaves
It means the car will run out of fuel on the road and stop for a long time
It means the grandparents will not recognize them at the door
It means the phone will never be found in the back of the car
questions.why: Since they are already running late, slow traffic uses up the small amount of time they have left.

wrong.B: The story does not mention running out of fuel.
wrong.C: Recognizing them is not a concern in the story.
wrong.D: Traffic has nothing to do with finding the phone.

questions.stem: Why does Omar stay calm instead of panicking when he talks to the worker?
options: He does not realize the train has left the station yet
He thinks the trip is not important anyway, so he does not mind
He wants to make his sister laugh by acting calm and funny
Staying calm helps him think clearly and ask for help
questions.why: By staying calm, Omar is able to clearly ask the worker the right question and get useful help.

wrong.A: Omar clearly knows the train has already left.
wrong.B: Omar cares a lot about reaching the coast.
wrong.C: Omar is focused on solving the problem, not joking.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events of the story?
options: By comparing two different train stations, one in a city and one in a village
By listing facts about trains around the world and how fast they travel
By telling events in order, from getting ready to boarding the last train
By jumping back and forth between two different holidays in the family's past
questions.why: The story moves in order: getting ready, the delay, the missed train, asking for help, and boarding the new one.

wrong.A: Only one station appears in the story.
wrong.B: The story is a narrative, not a list of facts.
wrong.D: The story does not jump between two holidays.

questions.stem: Why does the worker check his schedule carefully before answering?
options: He is bored and wants to waste time, so he looks at the paper slowly
He wants to give the children correct, accurate information
He forgot where the platforms are, so he must check the paper
He wants the family to miss the train, so he looks at it slowly
questions.why: Checking carefully helps the worker give the children the right platform and time, which helps them succeed.

wrong.A: The worker is helpful, not wasting time.
wrong.C: The worker clearly knows the station well.
wrong.D: The worker wants to help, not to cause them to miss it.

MID.prompt: Explain how the family's yearly habit of checking train times helped them, even though neither parent remembered to check it that day. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the habit helped the family.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The family's yearly habit of checking train times helped them even during the chaos of the missed train. Because they had practiced this every year, the children already knew how to read the busy arrivals board on their own. They also understood that different platforms lead to different parts of the country, so they were not confused when they needed to find a new one. This earlier practice meant that, even though the adults were distracted by the missing phone and traffic, the children still knew exactly what to do.

keyWords.definition: a period of time when something is made later than planned
keyWords.example: A long delay at the airport made us miss our connection.

keyWords.definition: a sudden feeling of strong fear or worry that makes it hard to think clearly
keyWords.example: She felt a wave of panic when she lost sight of her dog.

keyWords.definition: a list that shows the planned times for something, like trains or classes
keyWords.example: The coach printed a schedule showing every practice time.

keyWords.definition: the act of leaving, especially the time a vehicle leaves
keyWords.example: The departure board showed the next three flights.

keyWords.definition: a flat board with a clip at the top, used to hold papers while writing
keyWords.example: The nurse carried a clipboard with the patient's information.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: A single small mistake ruins the family's entire holiday plans completely
Children are rarely able to help during a real emergency
Years of quiet preparation let the children solve the problem calmly
The station worker solves the entire problem by himself alone
questions.why: The story shows that the children's years of learning to read schedules pay off the moment an emergency happens.

wrong.A: The family's holiday is not ruined; they still reach the coast.
wrong.B: The children are the ones who find the solution.
wrong.D: The worker only answers a question the children ask him.

questions.stem: What is the underlying cause of the family's narrow escape, beyond simply being late?
options: Years of learning to read schedules gave the children the skill to act fast
The train conveniently waited for the family at the correct platform that evening
The worker happened to be a close relative of the children
The weather had delayed every single train in the station
questions.why: The children's long practice with the schedule and platforms is what lets them act quickly once the crisis begins.

wrong.B: The train leaves on time; it does not wait for them.
wrong.C: The story never says the worker is related to the family.
wrong.D: The story does not mention weather delaying other trains.

questions.stem: In the story, the word schedule most nearly refers to —
options: a single ticket for one journey
the inside of a train car
a worker's personal opinion
a list showing when trains depart
questions.why: The worker checks his schedule to find departure times, meaning the printed list of trains and times.

wrong.A: A schedule is not a single ticket.
wrong.B: A schedule is not the inside of a train.
wrong.C: A schedule is a factual list, not an opinion.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that the children learned to read the board without help from their parents?
options: To suggest the parents never cared about the trip, and left everything to the children
To emphasize that the children's independent skill becomes essential later
To show that the parents are poor readers, so the children taught them
To explain why the train was delayed, since the parents were late to the station
questions.why: This detail sets up why the children, not the distracted adults, are the ones who solve the problem.

wrong.A: The parents clearly care about the trip and are stressed about it.
wrong.C: The parents can read; they are simply busy and distracted.
wrong.D: This detail is about the children's skill, not the delay's cause.

questions.stem: Based on the story, why does the family's careful yearly routine matter on this particular day?
options: It gives the children knowledge for when adults are distracted
It guarantees that absolutely nothing can ever go wrong again
It replaces the need for station workers
It means the family needs fewer tickets
questions.why: The yearly routine is what equips the children to act confidently the moment the adults are overwhelmed by the delay.

wrong.B: Things still go wrong this time, despite the routine.
wrong.C: The family still needs the worker's help to find the new platform.
wrong.D: The story does not suggest tickets are no longer needed.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they occur in the story.
options: The worker checks his schedule, the family leaves home, traffic slows the car
The family boards the new train, Dad loses his phone, traffic slows the car
Dad loses his phone, traffic slows the car, the worker checks his schedule
The worker checks his schedule, traffic slows the car, Dad loses his phone
questions.why: Dad first cannot find his phone, then traffic slows the drive, and finally the worker checks his schedule at the station.

wrong.A: The family leaves home before, not after, the worker checks his schedule.
wrong.B: They board the train only at the very end, not early on.
wrong.D: The phone goes missing before the drive, not after the worker is asked.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that the doors are already closing as the family boards?
options: To suggest the family boarded the wrong train by mistake at the station
To explain why the train was delayed overnight
To show that the worker closed the doors himself
To heighten the tension and emphasize how narrowly they succeed
questions.why: Closing doors create a dramatic, tense moment that shows just how close the family comes to missing the train again.

wrong.A: The story confirms this is the correct train.
wrong.B: The train is not described as delayed overnight.
wrong.C: The worker is not shown closing the doors.

questions.stem: The poll states that children can solve a family problem as well as adults can. How does the story's ending support or challenge this idea?
options: It challenges the idea, since only the parents solve the problem for the family, and the children do nothing
It supports the idea, since the children's question to the worker is what saves the trip
It is unrelated, since the worker solves the problem alone and the children watch
It challenges the idea, since the family misses the train anyway, and the children cry
questions.why: Omar's calm question to the worker is the key action that lets the whole family catch the last train, supporting the poll's claim.

wrong.A: It is Omar, a child, who asks the question that solves the problem.
wrong.C: The problem is clearly solved by the end of the story.
wrong.D: The family successfully catches the last train.

HIGH.prompt: The poll states that children can solve a family problem just as well as adults can. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about the preparation and actions of Sara and Omar.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that children can solve a family problem just as well as adults can, when they have the right preparation. Sara and Omar had spent years learning to read the arrivals board and understand the different platforms, so when the crisis hit, they were not starting from nothing. Omar's calm, clear question to the worker, rather than panic, is exactly what leads the family to the last train. Someone might argue that an adult's experience would always matter more in an emergency, but in this story the adults are the ones distracted by the missing phone and traffic, while the children's quieter, practiced knowledge is what actually saves the trip.

LOW.stem: Where do Sara and Omar's grandparents live?
options: In the big city
By the coast
On a high hill
Near the station
LOW.why: In the text, their grandparents live by the coast.

wrong.A: The family leaves the city to visit them.
wrong.C: The text does not say they live on a hill.
wrong.D: The family goes to the station to travel to them.

LOW.stem: Why is the road slow on the way to the station?
options: There are many cars.
Dad drives very slowly.
The road is closed.
It is raining hard.
LOW.why: The text says the road is slow because there are many cars.

wrong.B: Dad drives fast, not slow.
wrong.C: The text does not say the road is closed.
wrong.D: The text does not mention rain.

LOW.stem: In the story, the word board means —
options: a piece of wood
a seat on the train
a big sign with times
a ticket for the trip
LOW.why: The children learn to read the big board, and it shows every train.

wrong.A: A wood piece does not show train times.
wrong.B: The board is read, not sat on.
wrong.D: A ticket is small; the board is big and shows every train.

LOW.stem: What does Sara mean when she says they solved it together?
options: Dad drove the train.
The train was very late.
They are sad about the trip.
The family worked as a team.
LOW.why: Sara, Omar, and the family all helped them reach the last train, so they did it as a team.

wrong.A: Dad drove the car, not the train.
wrong.B: They catch the train just in time.
wrong.C: They sit down and smile, so they are happy.

MID.stem: Who hurries everyone out the door when Dad cannot find his phone?
options: Sara
Omar
The worker
Mom
MID.why: The text says Mom hurries everyone out the door and into the car.

wrong.A: Sara does not hurry the family out.
wrong.B: Omar is not the one who hurries them.
wrong.C: The worker is at the station, not at home.

MID.stem: Why does Sara gasp when she looks at the long list of times?
options: The station is very crowded.
She sees their train has left.
She cannot read the board.
The next train is too far away.
MID.why: She scans the list and learns that their train has already left without them.

wrong.A: The crowd is not why she gasps.
wrong.C: The children can read the board on their own.
wrong.D: She has not yet learned about another train.

MID.stem: In the story, the word dashes means —
options: runs very fast
walks slowly
sits down
looks around
MID.why: The family dashes toward the platform as fast as they can, so it means running quickly.

wrong.B: They are in a hurry, so they do not walk slowly.
wrong.C: They climb aboard soon after, not sit.
wrong.D: They are racing to the platform, not looking around.

MID.stem: Why does the author write that everything seems to go wrong at the same time?
options: To show the trip is easy
To say the family does not care
To tell about the grandparents
To show many problems pile up
MID.why: The lost phone, the rush, and the traffic all happen close together and build the problem.

wrong.A: Many things going wrong means the trip is not easy.
wrong.B: The family is worried, so they do care.
wrong.C: The sentence is about the problems, not the grandparents.

HIGH.stem: Where does the last train leave from?
options: The same platform as before
A platform right near the doors
A platform across the station
The platform next to the cars
HIGH.why: The worker says the train departs from a different platform across the station.

wrong.A: The first train had already left, and this is a different platform.
wrong.B: The text does not say it is near the doors.
wrong.D: No platform by the cars is mentioned.

HIGH.stem: Why does Dad glance repeatedly at the dashboard clock?
options: He is worried about the time.
He wants to stop and rest.
He is checking the car speed.
He is waiting for Mom to speak.
HIGH.why: The family is late and traffic crawls, so Dad keeps checking how little time is left.

wrong.B: Nothing says he wants to rest; he grips the wheel tightly.
wrong.C: The text says he looks at the clock, not a speed gauge.
wrong.D: Mom is not waiting to talk in the text.

HIGH.stem: In the story, the phrase "everything seems to unravel" most nearly means —
options: things get easier
things begin to fall apart
things move more slowly
things become quiet
HIGH.why: The lost phone, the delay, and the traffic show that the morning is going badly.

wrong.A: The problems make the day harder, not easier.
wrong.C: The family is rushing, not slowing down.
wrong.D: Traffic and worry make the scene stressful, not quiet.

HIGH.stem: Why might Sara sense trouble even before she reaches the board?
options: The board is broken.
Dad tells her bad news.
Few minutes are left.
The worker waves at her.
HIGH.why: The text says only a few precious minutes remain before departure, so she guesses they may be too late.

wrong.A: Nothing says the board is broken.
wrong.B: Dad does not tell her; she finds out herself.
wrong.D: She meets the worker later, through Omar.
